title: The Temple's Fall and the Coming of the Son of Man
summary: Leaving the temple, Jesus predicts that its buildings will be torn down, and on the Mount of Olives the disciples ask when this will happen and what will signal his coming and the end of the age. He warns of deceivers, wars, persecution, and a great tribulation linked to Daniel's abomination of desolation, and speaks of the Son of Man coming on the clouds. He tells them that no one knows the day or hour and calls them to stay awake and faithful like a servant whose master may return at any time.
story: Jesus has just pronounced that Jerusalem's house will be left desolate (23:38) and walked out of the temple for the last time. Now, looking back across the Kidron Valley at the temple from the Mount of Olives, he gives the last of the five great teaching blocks in Matthew, known as the Olivet discourse, which runs through chapter 25. Here the Gospel's story of Jesus' rejection by Jerusalem's leaders meets the larger story of God's judgment and the end of history. After it, the passion narrative begins in chapter 26. The discourse prepares the disciples for a world in which Jesus is absent, the temple falls, and they must bear witness under pressure.
historical:
The temple Jesus' disciples admired had been under reconstruction by Herod the Great since about 20 BC, with enormous white stone blocks and gold ornament; it was one of the wonders of the eastern Mediterranean. About forty years after Jesus spoke, Jewish resistance to Roman rule broke into open war (AD 66). Roman forces under Vespasian and then his son Titus besieged Jerusalem, and in AD 70 the city was taken and the temple burned and torn down. The Jewish historian Josephus, who was present with the Roman army, describes famine, factional fighting inside the city, false prophets promising deliverance, and terrible slaughter. The church historian Eusebius later recorded a tradition that the Christians of Jerusalem left the city before the war for Pella, east of the Jordan.

The phrase “the abomination of desolation” comes from Daniel (9:27, 11:31, 12:11). Jews in Jesus' day remembered its first fulfillment in 167 BC, when the Seleucid king Antiochus IV set up a pagan altar in the temple and sacrificed on it, as 1 Maccabees 1 records. The threat seemed to return in AD 40, when the emperor Gaius (Caligula) ordered a statue of himself set up in the temple, though he died before it happened. Messianic claimants and prophets who led crowds into the wilderness also appeared in the decades before the war; Acts mentions Theudas and an Egyptian who did so (Acts 5:36, 21:38).
cultural:
The language of the discourse belongs to apocalyptic, a way of speaking about God's decisive intervention in history common in Jewish writings of the period and rooted in books like Daniel. Its stock images, sun and moon darkened and stars falling, are drawn from the prophets, who used them for the fall of empires such as Babylon (Isaiah 13:10) and Edom (Isaiah 34:4). Readers disagree about how literally the cosmic signs are meant, but first hearers would have recognized them as the vocabulary of world-shaking judgment. The Son of Man coming on the clouds echoes Daniel 7:13-14, where one like a son of man comes before God and receives everlasting dominion.

The practical warnings reflect Judean life. Flat roofs were used as living space, with outside stairs, so someone on a roof could flee without going back inside. Winter rains swelled the wadis and made travel hard, and Sabbath travel was limited by custom and city gates might be shut. Grinding grain with a hand mill was daily women's work, often done in pairs, and a house was guarded by night through the watches into which the night was divided.
literary: The discourse answers a two-part question in verse 3: when will the temple be destroyed, and what will be the sign of Jesus' coming and the end of the age. How the answer is divided between those two parts is the main interpretive issue. The speech moves from general warnings (verses 4 to 14), to a specific crisis in Judea (15 to 28), to the coming of the Son of Man (29 to 31), to the lesson of the fig tree and the statement about this generation (32 to 35). Verse 36 then turns: no one knows the day or hour. From there to the end of chapter 25 the discourse becomes a series of parables about readiness: Noah's generation, the thief in the night, and the faithful and wicked servants. Repeated commands to watch, to not be deceived, and to endure run through the whole.

doctrines.note: Whatever the details, the chapter teaches that history is not a closed circle: the Son of Man will come in power and glory and gather his people. The church confesses in the creeds that Christ will come again to judge the living and the dead.
The fall of the temple is presented as God's judgment on the city that rejected his messengers, and the coming of the Son of Man brings a final sorting of the faithful and the unfaithful servant.
Before the end, the gospel of the kingdom will be preached in all the world as a testimony to all nations (verse 14). The waiting time is not empty; it is the time of witness.
The discourse calls for endurance, discernment against deceivers, and faithful work while the master is away. Readiness is shown by doing the work entrusted to you, not by calculating dates.

words.note: Parousia, presence or arrival. In the Greek world it was used for the visit of a ruler or official to a city, received with ceremony. Matthew is the only Gospel to use it, four times in this chapter, for the coming of the Son of Man, and it became the church's standard word for Christ's return.

Genea, generation. It usually means the people living at one time, and in Matthew often this generation that rejects Jesus (11:16, 23:36). In verse 34 most interpreters take it that way, which is why the statement is central to the debate about whether the preceding events belong to the first century. Some take it to mean a kind of people or the generation alive when the final signs begin.

Thlipsis, pressure, affliction, or tribulation. The word describes being crushed or squeezed. Verse 9 uses it of the disciples' suffering, and verse 21 speaks of a great tribulation unmatched in history. It is used across the New Testament for the ordinary suffering of believers as well as for particular crises.

Bdelygma, abomination, something detestable, especially in the sphere of worship. In the Greek Old Testament it often refers to idols or idolatrous practice. The phrase from Daniel points to a desecration of the holy place that leads to its desolation.

christ: The chapter shows Jesus as the prophet greater than the prophets and as the Son of Man of Daniel 7, who will come with the authority of God to gather his elect. He claims that his words will outlast heaven and earth (verse 35), a claim the Old Testament makes about the word of the Lord (Isaiah 40:8). At the same time he says that the Son does not know the day or hour (verse 36), a statement the church has read as part of his true humanity and his submission to the Father during his earthly ministry. The one who will come in glory is about to be handed over to be crucified, and the discourse holds both together.

hard.q: Does Matthew 24 describe the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70, the end of the world, or both?
hard.a: Faithful interpreters have read the discourse in several ways, and the question turns on verses 29 to 31 and 34. The first view, often called preterist (from the Latin for past), holds that everything through verse 35 was fulfilled in the first century. The cosmic signs are prophetic language for the collapse of a world order, as in Isaiah 13, and the Son of Man coming on the clouds draws on Daniel 7, where he comes to God to be vindicated and enthroned; the fall of the temple displays that vindication. Scholars such as R. T. France and N. T. Wright have argued forms of this reading, while still affirming Christ's future return taught in verses 36 onward and elsewhere. The second view is futurist: most or all of the discourse describes events still ahead, including a final tribulation, a future desecration, and the visible return of Christ. Many dispensational interpreters hold this view, and some read the one taken and the other left as a sudden removal of believers. The third view, probably the most common among commentators, sees both: the destruction of Jerusalem is fulfilled in the first century and serves as a pattern or foreshadowing of the final judgment, and the prophetic horizon holds near and far events together, as the Old Testament prophets often did. On every reading the church confesses that Christ will return bodily and in glory, and the chapter's own emphasis is that no one knows the hour, so the call is to watch and be faithful. The details are a second-order question on which Christians disagree in good faith.

questions: Jesus' first word in answer to the disciples' question about the end is a warning not to be deceived. Why do you think he starts there, and where are people deceived about these things today?
Verse 12 warns that the love of many will grow cold. What pressures cool love in a church or a person, and what keeps it warm?
The faithful servant is the one found doing his assigned work when the master returns. What work has been entrusted to you, and what would faithfulness look like this week?
